p.src: Now the Great Sage Sun pinched Sha Wujing with his left hand and Zhu Bajie with his right, and the two of them immediately understood. They sat aloft with blank faces, neither speaking nor stirring. Though the Daoists lit lamps and torches and examined them from front and back, the three looked exactly like gilded clay statues. Immortal Tiger Strength said, “If no villain came here, how were all the offerings eaten?” Immortal Deer Strength said, “It certainly looks like the work of men: everything with a skin was peeled, and every fruit with a stone had it spat out. Yet why can we see no human figure?” Immortal Antelope Strength said, “Brother, do not be suspicious. Perhaps our devout reverence—reciting scriptures here day and night, repeatedly presenting memorials, all in the name of the royal court—has surely moved the Celestial Worthies. It must be that the Three Pure Ones have descended in their holy persons and partaken of these offerings. Since the immortals have not yet returned and their august presence remains here, let us appeal to the Celestial Worthies for some holy water and golden elixir to present to His Majesty. Would that not grant him everlasting life and display the merit of our works?” Immortal Tiger Strength said, “You are right.” He ordered, “Disciples, strike up the music and chant the scriptures. Meanwhile, bring me my ritual robes, so that I may pace the celestial pattern and offer my prayers.” The young Daoists all obeyed and formed two orderly ranks. A chime rang with a clear clang, and together they recited one scroll of the True Scripture of the Yellow Court and the Way and Its Virtue. Immortal Tiger Strength donned his ritual robes and raised a jade tablet; dancing and stamping before the images, he prostrated himself and addressed those above:

The Pilgrim said, “All of you go outside the hall and close the lattice doors. You must not reveal the secrets of Heaven; then I shall leave you some holy water.” All the Daoists knelt below the vermilion steps and closed the doors of the hall.

p.src: At this time Tang Sanzang awoke and called, “Disciples, disciples! Attend me while I go to have our travel permit exchanged.” The Pilgrim, Sha Wujing, and Bajie hurriedly rose and dressed, then stood attending him on either side and said, “Master, allow us to report something. The ruler of this country believes those Daoists, promotes Daoism, and suppresses Buddhism. We fear that a misplaced word may make him refuse to exchange the travel permit, so we shall all enter court to protect you.” The Tang Monk was delighted and put on his brocade cassock. The Pilgrim took the travel documents, told Wujing to carry the alms bowl, and had Wuneng take the ringed staff; they entrusted their luggage and horse to the monks of Zhiyuan Monastery. They went straight to the Five Phoenix Tower, saluted the palace eunuch, gave their names, and explained that they were monks from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, journeying to fetch the scriptures, who had come to exchange their travel documents; they asked him to report their arrival. The gate commissioner entered the court, prostrated himself upon the golden steps, and reported, “Outside are four monks who say they have come from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures. They wish to exchange their travel documents and now await Your Majesty’s command before the Five Phoenix Tower.” On hearing the report, the king said, “These monks had nowhere else to seek death, so they have come here to seek it. Why did the patrol officers not arrest them and bring them here under guard?” The grand preceptor in attendance stepped out from the side and submitted, “The Great Tang of the Eastern Land lies in the Southern Continent of Jambudvipa and is known as the great realm of China. It is ten thousand li distant from here, and the road is infested with monsters. These monks must possess some magical powers, or they would never have dared journey westward. I beg Your Majesty, in consideration of these monks who have come so far from China, to summon them, examine their documents, and let them pass, so that the spirit of forming a good affinity may not be lost.” The king approved the memorial and summoned the Tang Monk and his companions before the Golden Throne Hall. Master and disciples formed a line before the steps, holding up the travel documents and presenting them to the king.

p.src: The king had only just unfolded the passport to examine it when a chamberlain came to report, “The three Imperial Preceptors have arrived.” In alarm, the king put away the passport, hastily descended from the Dragon Throne, ordered his attendants to set out embroidered stools, and personally bowed to welcome them. Tripitaka and his disciples turned to look and saw the great immortals swaggering straight in, followed by a pair of tousle-headed little acolytes with twin topknots. The officials in both ranks bowed so low that their backs arched, not daring to look up. They ascended the Golden Throne Hall and offered the king no salutation at all. The king said, “Imperial Preceptors, We did not summon you. What has moved you to condescend to visit Us today?” The old Daoist said, “We have come because there is a matter we must report. From what country are those four monks?” The king replied, “They were sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven and have come here to have their passport endorsed.” The three Daoists clapped their hands and laughed aloud. “We thought they had escaped, but here they still are!” Startled, the king asked, “What have the Imperial Preceptors to say about them? They only just reported their names, and We were about to seize them and send them for your use. But the Grand Preceptor attending Our carriage made a reasonable plea, so, considering how far they had come and unwilling to sever the good ties of China, We summoned them in to inspect their credentials. We did not expect you to question Us about them. Have they perhaps offended your august persons or wronged you in some way?” The Daoists laughed. “Your Majesty does not know. They arrived yesterday, killed two of our disciples outside the eastern gate, released five hundred imprisoned monks, and smashed the carts to pieces. At night they broke into our temple, destroyed the sacred images of the Three Pure Ones, and stole and ate the offerings bestowed by Your Majesty. They deceived us, and we took them for Heavenly Worthies descended to earth. We begged for some holy water and golden elixir to present to Your Majesty, hoping it would prolong your years and grant you immortality. Instead, they left us some urine and duped us with it. We each drank a mouthful and recognized the taste. Just as we were about to seize them, they fled. Now that they are still here today, it is truly as the saying goes: ‘Enemies are bound to meet on a narrow road.’” When the king heard this, he flew into a rage and was about to execute all four monks.

p.src: The Great Sage Sun pressed his palms together and cried out in a stern voice, “Your Majesty, pray calm your thunderous wrath for a moment and permit us monks to state our case.” The king said, “You have offended the Imperial Preceptors. How could their words contain any error?” Pilgrim said, “He claims that yesterday, outside the city, I killed two of his disciples. Who witnessed it? Even if we submit to this false charge, let two monks pay with their lives and allow the other two to continue their quest for the scriptures. He also says that I smashed the carts and freed the imprisoned monks. There are no witnesses to that either, and surely it does not warrant death, so let one more monk bear the penalty. But when he says that I destroyed the Three Pure Ones and caused havoc in the temple, that is a malicious accusation against me.” The king asked, “How is it a malicious accusation?” Pilgrim replied, “We monks are men of the Eastern Land and have only just arrived here. We do not even know our way through the streets, so how could we have known by night what was inside his temple? If someone really left urine there, they should have caught him on the spot. Instead, after all this time, they name us and seek to frame us. There are countless people in the world who assume false names and borrowed surnames. How can he say it was I? I beg Your Majesty to put aside your anger and investigate carefully.” The king was muddle-headed by nature, and after hearing Pilgrim’s argument, he could no longer reach a decision.

p.src: While he was still in doubt, another chamberlain came to report, “Your Majesty, many village elders are waiting outside to be summoned.” The king asked, “What business have they?” He immediately ordered that they be admitted. When they had been summoned before the hall, some thirty or forty village elders kowtowed toward the throne and said, “Your Majesty, no rain has fallen all spring this year, and we fear drought and famine in summer. We have come especially to petition you: please ask one of the venerable Imperial Preceptors to pray for a blessed rain and bring relief to all the people.” The king said, “Village elders, withdraw for now. Rain will soon come.” The village elders thanked him for his grace and departed. The king said, “Monks of the Tang court, do you know why We honor Daoism and suppress Buddhism? It is only because, when We prayed for rain in former years, the monks of Our realm could never summon so much as a single drop. Fortunately, Heaven sent down the Imperial Preceptors to rescue Us from misery. Now you have come from afar and offended the Imperial Preceptors. You ought to be punished at once, but We shall pardon you for the moment. Do you dare compete with Our Imperial Preceptor in praying for rain? If you can pray down a blessed rain and save the countless people, We shall pardon your offense, endorse your passport, and release you to journey west. But if you lose the contest and no rain falls, you shall all be dragged to the execution ground and put to death as a warning to the public.” Pilgrim laughed. “This humble monk also knows a little about praying for rain.”

p.src: Hearing this, the king immediately ordered the altar grounds to be swept and prepared. At the same time he commanded, “Prepare Our carriage. Tang Tripitaka, accompanied by Pilgrim, Sandy, and Pigsy, stood in attendance below the tower. The three Daoists sat beside the king in the tower. A short while later, an officer galloped up to report, “Everything at the altar is ready. May the venerable Imperial Preceptor ascend the platform.”

p.src: The Great Immortal Tiger Strength rose slightly, cupped his hands in farewell to the king, and went straight down from the tower. Pilgrim stepped forward to block his way and asked, “Where are you going, sir?” The Great Immortal replied, “To ascend the altar and pray for rain.” Pilgrim said, “You think rather too highly of yourself, refusing even to yield precedence to a monk from distant lands. Very well—it is just as they say: ‘Even a mighty dragon cannot subdue the local snake.’ You may go first, sir, but we must make the terms clear before the sovereign.” The Great Immortal asked, “What is there to make clear?” Pilgrim said, “If you and I both ascend the altar to pray for rain, how shall anyone know whether the rain is your doing or mine? It would be impossible to tell whose achievement it was.” Hearing this from above, the king was secretly delighted. “That little monk’s words do have some substance to them,” he thought. Sandy heard him and laughed inwardly. “He has a bellyful of schemes that he has not even begun to bring out yet.” The Great Immortal said, “There is no need to explain. His Majesty will naturally know.” Pilgrim replied, “Though His Majesty may know, I am a monk newly arrived from afar and have never met you before. If afterward each of us falsely claims the other’s merit, it will be an ugly business. We had better make everything clear before we begin.” The Great Immortal said, “Once I ascend the altar, simply take my command tablet as the signal: at its first strike, the wind will come; at the second, clouds will gather; at the third, thunder will roar and lightning flash together; at the fourth, rain will fall; and at the fifth, the clouds will disperse and the rain will cease.” Pilgrim laughed. “Marvelous! This monk has never seen such a thing. After you, then. After you.”

Hearing this from above, the king was secretly delighted. “That little monk’s words do have some substance to them,” he thought.
Sandy heard him and laughed inwardly. “He has a bellyful of schemes that he has not even begun to bring out yet.”
The Great Immortal said, “There is no need to explain. His Majesty will naturally know.”
Pilgrim replied, “Though His Majesty may know, I am a monk newly arrived from afar and have never met you before.
If afterward each of us falsely claims the other’s merit, it will be an ugly business. We had better make everything clear before we begin.”
The Great Immortal said, “Once I ascend the altar, simply take my command tablet as the signal: at its first strike, the wind will come;
at the second, clouds will gather;
at the third, thunder will roar and lightning flash together;
at the fourth, rain will fall;
and at the fifth, the clouds will disperse and the rain will cease.”
Pilgrim laughed. “Marvelous!
This monk has never seen such a thing.
After you, then. After you.”

p.src: The Great Immortal strode forward, with Tripitaka and the others following behind, and they went straight to the gate of the altar grounds. Looking up, they saw a high platform there, more than thirty feet tall. On either side of the platform stood banners of the Twenty-Eight Lunar Mansions. At the top stood a table bearing an incense burner, from which fragrant smoke curled in dense wisps. On both sides were two candlestands, their candles blazing brightly in the wind. Beside the burner leaned a golden tablet engraved with the name and title of the Thunder God. Below were five great vats, each filled to the brim with clear water. Willow branches floated upon the water, and each branch supported an iron tablet inscribed with talismanic characters of the Directorate of Thunder. To the left and right stood five great stakes, inscribed with the names of the barbarian thunder emissaries of the five directions. Beside every stake stood two Daoists, each holding an iron hammer and waiting to strike it. Behind the platform, many Daoists were busy writing official petitions. In the center stood a paper-burning furnace, together with several lifelike effigies representing the talisman-bearing emissaries and the local tutelary gods who assisted the rite.

p.src: The Great Immortal went in without the least ceremony and mounted straight to the high platform, where he took his place. At his side, a young Daoist held several yellow-paper talismans already inscribed and a precious sword, which he handed to the Great Immortal. Taking the precious sword, the Great Immortal recited an incantation and burned one talisman in the candle flame. Below, two or three Daoists brought forth a figurine holding a talisman and an official petition, and set fire to them as well. Then came the sharp crack of the command tablet above, and a gentle breath of wind could be seen drifting through the sky. Zhu Bajie muttered, “This is bad, this is bad! That Daoist really does have powers. The command tablet sounded once, and sure enough the wind began to blow.” The Pilgrim said, “Quiet, brothers. Say no more to me. Just look after Master while I go and take care of things.”

p.src: What a Great Sage! He plucked out a hair, breathed an immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It changed at once into a false Pilgrim, who stood beside Tang Sanzang. His true body sent forth its spirit, which sped into the sky and called loudly, “Who is in charge of the wind?” In alarm, Granny Wind clutched her bag shut and Young Lord Xun tied its mouth fast; then both came forward and saluted him. The Pilgrim said, “I am escorting the holy monk of the Tang court to the Western Heaven for scriptures. Passing through the Kingdom of Cart-Slow, I have wagered with that fiendish Daoist over who can pray down rain. Why do you help him instead of helping old Sun? I will spare you this time. Put away the wind. If so much as a breath stirs the Daoist’s beard, I shall give each of you twenty strokes of my iron cudgel.” Granny Wind said, “We would not dare! We would not dare!” And so not a breath of wind remained. Unable to contain himself, Bajie shouted, “Sir, you had better step down! The command tablet has sounded, yet why is there not the slightest breath of wind? Come down and let us go up.”

p.src: The Daoist again took up the command tablet, burned a talismanic dispatch, and struck it with another crack; at once clouds and mist filled the sky. The Great Sage Sun called out above them, “Who is spreading the clouds?” In alarm, the Cloud-Pushing Boy and the Mist-Spreading Lord came before him and saluted. The Pilgrim told them the whole story once more. The Cloud Boy and Mist Lord withdrew the clouds and mist, revealing the radiant sun; across ten thousand miles of sky, not a cloud remained. Bajie laughed and said, “This fellow is fit only to deceive the emperor and fob off the common people. He has no genuine skill at all. The command tablet has sounded twice, so why have no clouds appeared?”

p.src: Growing anxious, the Daoist gripped his precious sword, loosened his hair, chanted an incantation, burned another talisman, and brought the command tablet down once more. From the Southern Gate of Heaven, Celestial Lord Deng arrived in midair leading the Duke of Thunder and the Mother of Lightning, and they greeted the Pilgrim with due ceremony. The Pilgrim again explained all that had happened, then asked, “Why have you come with such earnest haste? Whose decree is this?” The Celestial Lord replied, “That Daoist’s Five-Thunder magic is genuine. He issued a petition and burned an official dispatch, thereby alerting the Jade Emperor. The Jade Emperor sent down a decree directly to the palace of the Celestial Worthy of Universal Transformation, Whose Thunder Resounds throughout the Nine Heavens. We have come by imperial command to bring thunder, lightning, and rain.” The Pilgrim said, “If that is so, all of you wait here for now and follow old Sun’s lead.” And sure enough, the thunder ceased to rumble and the lightning ceased to flash.

p.src: The Daoist grew more frantic still. He added incense, burned talismans, chanted incantations, and struck the command tablet again. In midair, the Dragon Kings of the Four Seas arrived together in a great company. The Pilgrim shouted down at them, “Ao Guang, where are you going?” Ao Guang, Ao Shun, Ao Qin, and Ao Run came forward and saluted him. The Pilgrim again explained the whole affair, then said, “I troubled you the other day, but we did not succeed. In today’s business, I hope you will lend me your aid.” The Dragon Kings replied, “At your command, at your command.” The Pilgrim then thanked Ao Shun, saying, “The other day I was indebted to your son for binding the monster and rescuing my master.” The Dragon King said, “That wretch remains chained beneath the sea. I have not dared deal with him on my own and was just going to ask the Great Sage to decide his fate.” The Pilgrim said, “Deal with him however you please. For now, just help me accomplish this one task. That Daoist has now finished sounding the command tablet four times, so it is old Sun’s turn to go up and act. But I do not know how to issue talismans, burn dispatches, or strike any command tablet, so all of you must help me carry it through.” Celestial Lord Deng said, “Who would dare disobey the Great Sage’s instructions? But we must have a signal before we dare act according to your command. Otherwise the thunder and rain will fall into disorder, and it will seem that the Great Sage has no proper method.” The Pilgrim said, “I shall use my cudgel as the signal.” The Duke of Thunder cried in alarm, “Grandfather! How could we endure a blow from that cudgel?” The Pilgrim said, “I am not going to strike you. Just watch: when I point this cudgel upward, the wind must blow.” Granny Wind and Young Lord Xun answered eagerly, “We shall release the wind at once.” “At the second point of the cudgel, the clouds must spread.” The Cloud-Pushing Boy and Mist-Spreading Lord said, “We shall spread the clouds at once! Do not be late or disobey.”

p.src: Having finished his instructions, he lowered his cloud, shook the hair, and took it back onto his body. Those mortals of fleshly eyes understood none of this. The Pilgrim called loudly from the side, “Sir, if you please! All four strokes of the command tablet have sounded, yet there is still no wind, cloud, thunder, or rain. It is time to yield the platform to me.” The Daoist had no choice. Not daring to occupy the platform any longer, he descended and yielded it to him. Pursing his lips, he went straight up to the tower to appear before the king. The Pilgrim said, “Let me follow him and hear what he has to say.” He heard the king ask, “I have been listening here with the utmost attention. Your command tablet sounded four times, yet neither wind nor rain appeared. Why is that?” The Daoist replied, “Today all the dragon gods are away from home.” The Pilgrim cried sternly, “Your Majesty, all the dragon gods are at home. It is only that this Imperial Preceptor’s magic is powerless, and he cannot summon them. Wait until this monk summons them, and you shall see.” The king said, “Go at once and mount the altar. I shall remain here and await the rain.”

p.src: Having received the decree, the Pilgrim hurried back to the altar, pulled Tang Sanzang by the arm, and said, “Master, please mount the platform.” Tang Sanzang said, “Disciple, but I do not know how to pray for rain.” Bajie laughed and said, “He has landed you in trouble! p.src: The king ordered the imperial carriage to return, intending to exchange the travel rescript and send the Tang Monk on his way. If one traces the matter to its root, it was still I who summoned the dragons and caused the rain. How can it be counted as his merit?” The muddle-headed king heard this and once again wavered, unable to decide.

The king said, “Thank you for troubling your noble selves to descend here. You may now return.

The Pilgrim said, “Divine ones, each of you may return to your own abode. The king will hold a rite of thanksgiving on another day.”
The Dragon Kings returned directly to their seas, and all the other gods went back to Heaven.
